gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the new TEAC W-1200 and Tascam 202MKVII are rated at 0.25% WRMS wow and flutter. That is about 13 times the Nakamichi Dragon's rated 0.019% WRMS (0.25 / 0.019 = 13.2) and 6 to 25 times the 0.01–0.042% RMS that reviewers measured on the Revox B215.
standout_why: StereoNET (cited, 2026-08-25) gives no flutter figure for any deck. It says only that new players sit 'a healthy step behind' serviced vintage units. It also gives no dubbing speed or USB format, and prices the W-1200 at about $549. The Tape Lab page (tapelab.live, cited) has no numbers at all, only phrases like 'mid-price' and 'rack-mountable'. Portcycling (cited in one chat) blocked the fetch (HTTP 403), so I couldn't check it. In all three chats ChatGPT said the new decks are 'not as high-fidelity' as vintage flagships but gave no number.
decides: This backs ChatGPT's split and puts a number on it. If sound quality is the goal, a serviced vintage 3-head deck is the pick, because the W-1200 and 202MKVII flutter is roughly an order of magnitude higher. If the goal is warranty, dubbing and USB digitizing, the W-1200 is still the new-deck pick: it is lighter and has a remote. Both new decks share the same 0.25% transport rating and 48 kHz/16-bit USB, so the choice between the two comes down to rack ears versus home use, not sound.

findings.label: Wow and flutter (measured by reviewers)
findings.note: Wikipedia quoting Roberson 1985 p. 52, Stark 1988 p. 56, Stark 1986 p. 42 and Feldman 1986 p. 18. The maker's rating is 0.1% maximum (Studer Service Instructions 1985, sec. 7.4), which is not the same measure as WRMS. Ratio: 0.25 / 0.042 = 6.0×; 0.25 / 0.01 = 25×. Rated frequency response is 30–20,000 Hz for Type II/IV, against 15 kHz for the W-1200 on Type II (a 5 kHz higher ceiling). Launch price was $1,390 (Stereo Review, Mar 1985).
